newsitem.title: POLAND: Warsaw bourse seen inching down before large sales.
newsitem.headline: Warsaw bourse seen inching down before large sales.

text.p: The Warsaw bourse should extend this week's slight downtrend next week as forthcoming large privatisations could hurt the secondary market, analysts said.

Poland's largest commercial bank, Bank Handlowy SA, was cleared for public trade on Wednesday and is scheduled for sale in late May, while copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz's privatisation is seen taking place in June. @

"We can have falls, mainly connected with Handlowy and KGHM ....Handlowy's domestic retail tranche will be about 500 million zlotys, it's a lot of money and it's just one tranche," said Czeslaw Pospieszynski, an analyst at PBI brokerage.
Analysts said that in the longer-term, until parliamentary elections this September, the bourse could form a horizontal trend with phases of growth and falls.
The main market's all-share WIG index fell 0.7 percent this week to 16,424.2 points. @
Analysts said next Thursday's inflation figure for April should be low, at about 0.7 percent, but said that high market rates meant that April's number was unlikely to immediately help the market.

Analysts said the banking sector continued its weak performance this week amid little hope for an earnings rebound after an unspectacular first quarter, but some expected banks to rebound or at least stop falling in the next few sessions.
They said some banks already looked attractive at current prices, with some trading more than 30 percent below their 52-week highs two and a half month ago. @

"Some banks' prices already look attractive, but they might still fall a little, although they surely are in the zone of attractive valuation," said Pawel Tarnowski, an analyst at Raiffeisen Capital and Investment Polska.
Kredyt Bank was this week's biggest loser, falling 11.8 percent.
Long-neglected garment makers attracted investor interest this week, with Prochnik's 44-percent surge leading the main market. @

But analysts said this sector's growth possibly reflected speculation caused by the stocks' low price earnings ratios against the overall market, which they said were justified given the sector's poor prospects.
Analysts said more speculative swings were likely in ailing Espebepe before the builder's creditors meet next Friday to decide on whether it will have its debts written-off or go bankrupt.
